To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
family history of breast or hematopoietic cancer was associated with increased incidence of adult acute leukemia.

a family history of cancer might be a surrogate for a susceptibility gene, and that a family history for breast cancer was associated with increased leukemia risk in the presence of exposure to a range of environmental exposures.
family history of breast or ovarian cancer was associated with increased risk of adult acute leukemia, and that this association was modified by occupational and other environmental exposures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction between exposures and family history of breast cancers on the incidence of adult acute leukemia.
the role of family history of breast and hematopoietic cancer as markers of susceptibility to exposures and the potential synergy of exposures in the etiology of adult acute leukemia.
the interaction between family history of breast and leukemia risk factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a history of breast cancer among relatives is associated with a significantly increased risk of acute leukemia, and that the effect is enhanced in the presence of a range of exposures.
family history of breast is associated with an increased incidence of leukemia in the presence of a range of environmental exposures.

the risk of adult acute leukemia is increased by family history of breast and hematologic malignancies and that this effect is modified by a number of exposures, including ever-smoking, general solvent exposure, aromatic hydrocarbons, and diagnostic ionizing radiations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
family history of breast and leukemia is associated with an increased risk of adult acute leukemia, but this is not the result of any single risk factor.
family history of breast is a marker of susceptibility for adult acute leukemia.
family history of breast and hematopoietic cancer might be a risk factor for adult acute leukemia, possibly because of an interaction with other risk factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the interaction of a family history and an environmental exposure may not necessarily be a multiplicative interaction, but rather an additive interaction, which is more difficult to detect in a case-control study.
family history of breast cancers might be a marker that identifies individuals who are at increased risk of leukemia because of their susceptibility to exposures.
family history is a marker for a range of exposures and that the effects of the exposures are not simply additive but are instead synergistic.
